{{Short description|Minimum monochromatic-triangle theorem in graph theory}}

In [[graph theory]], '''Goodman's theorem''' gives the exact minimum number of monochromatic triangles in a two-coloring of the edges of a [[complete graph]]. If the edges of <math>K_n</math> are colored red or blue, the minimum depends on <math>n</math> modulo four. A. W. Goodman published the result in 1959, phrasing the two colors as pairs of acquaintances and strangers at a party. Forms of the result are also known as '''Goodman's formula'''.{{sfn|Goodman|1959|pp=778–783}}{{sfn|Grzesik|Lee|Lidický|Volec|2022|p=908}}

The proof counts pairs of differently colored edges incident with each vertex and reduces the lower bound to a degree calculation. Dividing the exact minimum by the total number of triangles gives a limiting proportion of <math>1/4</math>, the same as the expected monochromatic proportion in a uniformly random red–blue coloring. In [[Ramsey theory]] this says that <math>K_3</math> is a [[common graph]]. Goodman also proved a related inequality between edge and triangle [[homomorphism density|homomorphism densities]]. Later work determined the three-color minimum for all sufficiently large complete graphs and the four-color asymptotic minimum.{{sfn|Cummings et al.|2013|pp=489–490}}{{sfn|Zhao|2023|pp=173–174}}{{sfn|Kiem|Pokutta|Spiegel|2026|loc=Theorem 1}}

== Statement ==
Let <math>M(K_3,n)</math> be the minimum number of unlabeled monochromatic copies of <math>K_3</math> among all red–blue edge-colorings of <math>K_n</math>. Goodman's theorem states that{{sfn|Goodman|1959|pp=778–783}}{{sfn|Sane|Wallis|1988|p=197}}

<math display="block">M(K_3,n)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{n(n-2)(n-4)}{24}, & n\text{ even},\\[6pt]
\displaystyle \frac{n(n-1)(n-5)}{24}, & n\equiv 1\pmod 4,\\[6pt]
\displaystyle \frac{(n+1)(n-3)(n-4)}{24}, & n\equiv 3\pmod 4.
\end{cases}</math>

Each of the three bounds is attainable.{{sfn|Sane|Wallis|1988|p=197}} A. J. Schwenk later gave the equivalent single expression{{sfn|Schwenk|1972|pp=1113–1117}}

<math display="block">M(K_3,n)
={n\choose 3}
-\left\lfloor
\frac n2\left\lfloor\frac{(n-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor
\right\rfloor.</math>

The first nonzero value is <math>M(K_3,6)=2</math>. Thus the [[theorem on friends and strangers]], which guarantees a monochromatic triangle in every red–blue coloring of <math>K_6</math>, can in this case be strengthened to two monochromatic triangles.{{sfn|Goodman|1959|pp=778–783}}{{sfn|Sane|Wallis|1988|p=197}}

As <math>n</math> tends to infinity,

<math display="block">\frac{M(K_3,n)}{{n\choose3}}\longrightarrow\frac14.</math>

A fixed triangle in a uniformly random red–blue edge-coloring is monochromatic with probability <math>2(1/2)^3=1/4</math>. The deterministic minimum therefore has the same limiting density as the random-coloring expectation.{{sfn|Cummings et al.|2013|pp=489–490}}{{sfn|Zhao|2023|p=173}}

== Proof ==
For a vertex <math>v</math>, let <math>r_v</math> and <math>b_v</math> be its red and blue degrees. Then <math>r_v+b_v=n-1</math>. The product <math>r_vb_v</math> counts unordered pairs of differently colored edges incident with <math>v</math>. Every nonmonochromatic triangle contributes such a pair at exactly two of its vertices, while a monochromatic triangle contributes none. If <math>N</math> is the number of nonmonochromatic triangles, double counting gives

<math display="block">2N=\sum_v r_vb_v.</math>

Consequently, if <math>T</math> is the number of monochromatic triangles, then{{sfn|Goodman|1959|pp=779–781}}{{sfn|Ehrenborg|2021|pp=383–386}}

<math display="block">T={n\choose3}-\frac12\sum_v r_vb_v
={n\choose3}-\frac12\sum_v r_v(n-1-r_v).</math>

The product is largest when the two degrees are as close as the integer and parity constraints permit. If <math>n=2m</math>, then <math>r_vb_v\leq m(m-1)</math> for every vertex, and hence

<math display="block">T\geq {n\choose3}-\frac n2m(m-1)
=\frac{n(n-2)(n-4)}{24}.</math>

Now suppose <math>n</math> is odd and put <math>q=(n-1)/2</math>. For each vertex,

<math display="block">r_v(n-1-r_v)=q^2-(r_v-q)^2.</math>

If <math>n\equiv1\pmod4</math>, the pointwise bound <math>r_vb_v\leq q^2</math> gives

<math display="block">T\geq {n\choose3}-\frac{nq^2}{2}
=\frac{n(n-1)(n-5)}{24}.</math>

If <math>n\equiv3\pmod4</math>, then <math>q</math> and <math>n</math> are both odd. The red graph cannot have degree <math>q</math> at every vertex, because its degree sum would be odd, contrary to the [[handshaking lemma]]. Thus <math>\sum_v(r_v-q)^2\geq1</math>, so

<math display="block">T\geq {n\choose3}-\frac{nq^2-1}{2}
=\frac{(n+1)(n-3)(n-4)}{24}.</math>

These arguments establish the three lower bounds. Colorings attaining them exist in every case, so the bounds give the exact minimum.{{sfn|Goodman|1959|pp=779–783}}{{sfn|Sane|Wallis|1988|p=197}} The floor functions in Schwenk's expression encode the same two integer restrictions: the largest value of a single product <math>r_vb_v</math> and, when <math>n\equiv3\pmod4</math>, the parity obstruction on the degree sum.{{sfn|Schwenk|1972|pp=1113–1117}}

== Graph and density formulations ==
A red–blue coloring of <math>K_n</math> can be represented by a simple graph <math>G</math>, with the red edges taken as <math>E(G)</math> and the blue edges as the edges of the [[complement graph]] <math>\overline G</math>. If <math>\tau(G)</math> denotes the number of unlabeled triangles in <math>G</math>, the counting identity becomes

<math display="block">\tau(G)+\tau(\overline G)
={n\choose3}-\frac12\sum_{v\in V(G)}d_G(v)\bigl(n-1-d_G(v)\bigr).</math>{{sfn|Goodman|1959|pp=779–781}}{{sfn|Ehrenborg|2021|pp=383–386}}

Thus the combined number of triangles in a graph and its complement is determined by the degree sequence. The lower-bound part of Goodman's theorem is therefore a degree optimization; the separate attainability statement ensures that the optimum degree patterns needed for the three congruence cases can be realized by colorings.

In graph-limit notation, the asymptotic two-color consequence is the graphon inequality{{sfn|Zhao|2023|p=173}}

<math display="block">t(K_3,W)+t(K_3,1-W)\geq\frac14.</math>

Here <math>W</math> and <math>1-W</math> represent the two color classes, and <math>t(K_3,W)</math> is the triangle homomorphism density. The constant graphon <math>W=1/2</math> attains equality. A different inequality attributed to Goodman, and also discussed under his name in the homomorphism-density setting, relates the triangle and edge densities of a single graphon:{{sfn|Zhao|2023|p=174}}

<math display="block">t(K_3,W)\geq t(K_2,W)\bigl(2t(K_2,W)-1\bigr).</math>

The first inequality is the asymptotic form of the monochromatic-triangle problem; the second fixes one graphon and bounds its triangle density from its edge density.

== Ramsey multiplicity and multicolor extensions ==
For a graph <math>H</math> and a positive integer <math>k</math>, let <math>M_k(H,n)</math> be the minimum number of monochromatic unlabeled copies of <math>H</math> among all <math>k</math>-edge-colorings of <math>K_n</math>. Goodman's theorem gives <math>M_2(K_3,n)</math> exactly. Its limiting value of <math>1/4</math> agrees with the random two-color benchmark, which is the statement that the triangle is a common graph.{{sfn|Cummings et al.|2013|pp=489–490}}{{sfn|Grzesik|Lee|Lidický|Volec|2022|pp=907–908}}{{sfn|Zhao|2023|p=173}}

Goodman considered the three-color analogue in 1985. He did not determine the minimum total number of monochromatic triangles, but obtained sharp bounds for related combinations of triangle types.{{sfn|Goodman|1985|loc=Abstract}} In 2013, James Cummings, Daniel Král', Florian Pfender, Konrad Sperfeld, Andrew Treglown, and Michael Young determined the three-color minimum for all sufficiently large <math>n</math>. If <math>n=5m+r</math> with <math>0\leq r\leq4</math>, their result gives{{sfn|Cummings et al.|2013|loc=Theorem 2 and Corollary 3}}

<math display="block">M_3(K_3,n)
=r{m+1\choose3}+(5-r){m\choose3}</math>

for all sufficiently large <math>n</math>, and hence an asymptotic monochromatic-triangle density of <math>1/25</math>. Their proof combines a flag-algebra calculation with a probabilistic argument.{{sfn|Cummings et al.|2013|p=491}}

For four colors, Aldo Kiem, Sebastian Pokutta, and Christoph Spiegel proved in 2026 that the asymptotic minimum is <math>1/256</math> of all triangles. They also showed that every sufficiently large extremal coloring is based on a blow-up of one of the two triangle-free three-colorings of <math>K_{16}</math>; their proof uses a flag-algebra formulation and stability arguments.{{sfn|Kiem|Pokutta|Spiegel|2026|loc=Abstract and Theorem 1}}
